parts.title: My first debate
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last term, my teacher asked me to join the school debating team. I said no at first, because I hate speaking in front of people. But she told me that I was good at arguing with my brother, so I decided to try.

Our first debate was against another school, and the subject was "Zoos should be closed". We were given the side against zoos. I did not agree with it, but our coach said that a good debater can argue for any idea. This surprised me.

I spoke second. My notes were shaking in my hands, and my voice was a whisper. But after a minute, I forgot my nerves and started to enjoy myself. I gave three reasons and an example, and I looked at the judges, as I had been taught.

We lost the debate, but one of the judges said that my speech was the clearest. That made me happy. I have learned that listening is just as important as speaking, and I now understand other people's opinions much better.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer decide to join the team?
options: Her friends were all in it
She wanted to win a prize
questions.explanation: Her teacher said she was good at arguing with her brother.

questions.prompt: What surprised her about the subject?
options: She had to argue for an idea she disliked
The topic was far too easy for her
The other school did not arrive on time
questions.explanation: She did not agree with her side, but a good debater can argue for any idea.

questions.prompt: How did she feel when she began to speak?
questions.explanation: Her notes were shaking and her voice was a whisper.

questions.prompt: What happened after a minute?
questions.explanation: She forgot her nerves and started to enjoy herself.

questions.prompt: What has she learned?
options: Judges are always right about everything
Winning is the most important thing of all
Listening is as important as speaking
questions.explanation: Listening is just as important as speaking.

parts.title: How to give a good speech
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Many people are afraid of speaking in public, but it is a skill that anyone can learn. [1] Here are some simple tips to help you.

First, know your audience. Think about who will be listening and what they want to hear. [2] A talk to young children, for example, should be very different from a talk to teachers.

Second, keep it short and clear. Most listeners remember only two or three main ideas. [3] Everything else just makes your message harder to follow.

Third, speak slowly. When we are nervous, we speak very fast. [4] Take a breath at the end of each sentence, and you will sound much more confident.

Finally, practise out loud. Stand in front of a mirror, or ask a friend to listen. [5] The more you rehearse, the less afraid you will be on the day.
sentences: Choose these carefully and repeat them at the end.
It may feel strange at first, but it really works.
The same words will not work for every group of people.
This makes it difficult for the audience to understand you.
All it takes is a little preparation and a lot of practice.
Do not forget to wear comfortable shoes.

gaps.explanation: All it takes is a little preparation, and the next sentence gives tips.
The same words will not work for every group, and the example follows.
Choose the main ideas carefully; everything else makes the message harder.
Fast speech makes it hard to understand, and the next sentence advises taking a breath.
It may feel strange, and the next sentence says the more you rehearse the less afraid you are.

parts.title: A note about the debate
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Dear Lena, I just wanted to say congratulations on your speech yesterday! You were so calm and clear that nobody could [1] that you were nervous. I especially liked the part [2] you told the story about your first day at school. Everyone laughed, and I think that this helped the judges to [3] you. Our team did not win, [4] I am sure that we will do better next time. Mrs Blake said that we should practise our answers to difficult questions. I [5] already started to write mine. Are you free on Thursday after lessons? We could meet in the library and work together [6] our next debate. See you soon, Jory

parts.title: A great speaker
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Martin Luther King was one of the greatest speakers in history. He gave his most famous speech in 1963, [1] he spoke to more than two hundred thousand people in Washington. He talked about his dream that one day, all people would be treated [2] the same. He did not read from paper for most of the speech. Instead, he spoke from his heart, [3] his voice rose and fell like music. He also used short, simple sentences and repeated the words "I have a dream" again and again. This made it easy for people to remember. Speech experts say that his talk is a perfect example [4] how to speak in public. Thousands of students study it every year, and many people can still say parts of it by heart. His words continue to inspire people all [5] the world, long after his death. It shows that a good speech can change the way people think, and this is [6] we remember it today.

gaps.explanation: In 1963, when he spoke to 200,000 people: relative of time.
Treated the same: a fixed phrase.
He spoke from his heart, and his voice rose and fell.
An example of how to speak: a fixed phrase.
All over the world: a fixed phrase.
This is why we remember it: the reason.

parts.title: A talk about a debating competition
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I am Lena, the captain of the school debating team. Today I would like to tell you about our competition next month. It will be held in the town hall on the fourteenth of November. Teams of three students from eight schools will take part. Each speaker has four minutes, and then there is a break of two minutes. The topic is given only one hour before the debate, so there is not much time to prepare. We will be told which side to argue for just before we begin. Three judges will give marks for clear ideas, good manners and teamwork. The winning team will receive a silver cup and will go on to the national final in the capital. If you want to watch, entry is free, but you must arrive by half past nine. Please remember to switch off your mobile phones. Thank you for listening.

gaps.prompt: The competition is on the ___ of November
gaps.explanation: It will be held on the fourteenth of November.
Teams of three students from eight schools.

gaps.prompt: The topic is given ___ hour before the debate
gaps.explanation: The topic is given only one hour before.
The winning team will receive a silver cup.

gaps.prompt: Visitors must arrive by half past ___
gaps.explanation: You must arrive by half past nine.

parts.title: An interview with a debating coach
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Keir, you coach the national schools debating team. What do you like about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I love seeing shy students find their voice. Some arrive unable to speak in front of ten people, and a year later they speak to hundreds.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you teach first?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Listening. A debater who does not listen cannot answer the other side. Then we work on building arguments with clear examples.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do students always argue for what they believe?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not usually. They are given a side, and they must defend it. It teaches them to understand ideas they disagree with.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the most common mistake?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Speaking too fast and trying to say too much. A few strong points are better than twenty weak ones.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you prepare for a competition?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: We practise answering surprise questions. We also hold a mock debate the day before, and I play the judge.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do students gain from debating?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Confidence, of course, but also respect for other opinions. Many of them tell me that it has helped them in every subject.

questions.explanation: Listening comes first.

questions.explanation: It teaches them to understand ideas they disagree with.

questions.prompt: What is the most common mistake?
